findings.title: Dynamic zod keys via .toString() don't validate anything meaningful
findings.body: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses computed property keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` intending (per the comment) to allow any numeric property to pass as the expiry and allow other properties through. However, calling `.toString()` on a Zod schema instance does not produce a wildcard matcher — it produces a fixed, identical string literal for both expressions (Zod schemas don't override toString()), so both computed keys collapse onto the same literal key, and the second (optional/unknown) overwrites the first. The resulting schema is effectively just `{ access_token: string }`. Because Zod objects strip unrecognized keys from the parsed result by default, every other field returned by a self-hosted credential-sync endpoint (expiry, refresh_token, etc.) is silently discarded whenever APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set. This defeats the entire purpose of the sync feature: expiry/refresh data never survives the parse.

findings.title: Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"
findings.body: When the parsed refresh response has no `refresh_token` field, the code sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"` — a hardcoded placeholder string, not the previously stored refresh token. This path runs for both sync and non-sync refresh flows (e.g. office365calendar and zoomvideo call parseRefreshTokenResponse with the raw refresh-response object as the schema input). Many OAuth providers do not re-issue a new refresh_token on every access-token refresh, so this code will silently overwrite a user's valid refresh token with the garbage string "refresh_token" in the database, permanently breaking that calendar/video integration until the user reconnects the app. There is no fallback to the existing credential's refresh_token value.

findings.title: refreshOAuthTokens returns an un-parsed fetch Response, but many callers expect `.data` or a final token object
findings.body: When app credential sync is enabled, refreshOAuthTokens returns the raw, unread `fetch` Response object from CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT. Callers are inconsistent in what they expect: googlecalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts does `const token = res?.data;` (expects an axios-like object with `.data`), hubspot/lib/CalendarService.ts assigns the return value directly to a `HubspotToken` (expects a parsed token object, not a Response), and zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts & zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts both do `tokenInfo.data.error`/`tokenInfo.data.expiryDate` (expect an axios response shape). A plain fetch Response has none of these, so when sync is enabled these call sites will throw TypeErrors (reading properties of undefined) or silently store corrupted/empty credential keys. Only providers that explicitly call `.json()`/`handleErrorsJson` on the result (office365calendar, office365video, zoomvideo, webex, lark) work correctly with this return shape.

findings.title: `prisma` is used without being imported, breaking compilation/runtime
findings.body: The new refresh-token logic in getClient() calls `await prisma.credential.update(...)`, but this file never imports `prisma` (no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"` was added despite the new usage). This will fail TypeScript type-checking ("Cannot find name 'prisma'") and, if it somehow passes a build, will throw a ReferenceError at runtime the first time a Salesforce credential needs a token refresh, breaking the Salesforce integration entirely.

findings.title: Salesforce token refresh bypasses refreshOAuthTokens, so credential sync never applies to Salesforce
findings.body: Unlike every other updated provider (google, hubspot, office365, zoho-bigin, zohocrm, zoom, webex), the Salesforce CalendarService calls `fetch("https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token", ...)` directly instead of going through `refreshOAuthTokens`. As a result, even when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are configured, Salesforce token refresh will always hit Salesforce directly and never use the self-hoster's sync endpoint, silently excluding Salesforce from the feature this PR advertises.

findings.title: Fragile success check using response.statusText instead of response.ok
findings.body: `if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw new HttpError(...)` relies on the HTTP reason phrase being exactly the string "OK". Depending on the runtime/fetch implementation (e.g. HTTP/2 responses or certain fetch polyfills), statusText can be empty or differ even for a successful 200 response, causing valid refresh responses to be incorrectly treated as errors. `response.ok` (or checking `response.status`) is the standard, reliable way to detect failures.

findings.title: Webhook secret comparison is not constant-time
findings.body: The shared-secret check `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` uses a plain string inequality comparison. This is vulnerable to timing attacks that can let an attacker incrementally guess the secret by measuring response-time differences. A constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on buffers of equal length) should be used for secret/token verification on a publicly reachable endpoint.

findings.title: Ambiguous credential lookup can overwrite the wrong credential
findings.body: `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` does not disambiguate between multiple credentials a user may have for the same app (e.g. multiple Google Calendar or Office365 accounts connected under the same appId). If more than one credential row matches, `findFirst` picks an arbitrary one and the subsequent `update` will overwrite that record's `key`, potentially corrupting an unrelated, working connection for a different account than the one the self-hoster intended to sync. The request schema has no way to target a specific credential (e.g. an external account id), making this unsafe for any app that supports multiple accounts per user.

findings.title: No HTTP method restriction on the webhook handler
findings.body: The handler does not check `req.method`, so GET/PUT/DELETE requests are processed identically to POST. For non-POST requests the body will typically be empty/invalid, causing the unguarded `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` call to throw, which is not caught anywhere in the handler and will surface as an unhandled exception/500 instead of a clean 405 Method Not Allowed response.

findings.title: Redirect URI hardcoded instead of derived from appConfig.slug
findings.body: This change replaces `WEBAPP_URL + \`/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback\`` with a hardcoded `WEBAPP_URL + \`/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback\``, while `zoho-bigin/api/callback.ts` still builds its redirect URI dynamically from `appConfig.slug`. This introduces an inconsistency: if `appConfig.slug` ever changes, the authorize URL and the token-exchange redirect URI will diverge, breaking the OAuth flow (redirect_uri mismatch errors from the provider). This change is unrelated to the credential-sync feature and appears to be an unintended regression.

findings.title: No automated tests for the new credential-sync webhook or token-refresh helpers
findings.body: This PR introduces a new externally reachable webhook endpoint that decrypts and writes arbitrary third-party OAuth credentials into the database, plus shared helpers (parseRefreshTokenResponse, refreshOAuthTokens) used across nine app integrations. None of this new, security- and data-integrity-sensitive logic has accompanying unit/integration tests (the PR description explicitly states no tests were added), despite the bugs identified in parseRefreshTokenResponse/refreshOAuthTokens that tests would likely have caught.
